declaredAssumptions: Gravity is constant and acts vertically downward.

itemLevelCitations.locator: Section 15.4, nonlinear pendulum equation and equations 15.17–15.19
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: The gravity restoring term −(g/L)sin(theta), small-angle approximation and undamped T0=2pi sqrt(L/g), omega0=sqrt(g/L)

itemLevelCitations.locator: Section 15.1, simple harmonic motion and linear restoring-force discussion
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: Small-angle linearization as a harmonic oscillator
itemLevelCitations.limitations: General SHM material is not a calibration or validation source for the nonlinear damped pendulum implementation.

declaredAssumptions: The bob is treated as a point mass on a massless, inextensible rod/string of fixed length with a frictionless pivot.
The gravity torque is represented by the exact nonlinear sin(theta) term.
Damping is represented phenomenologically as a linear angular-velocity term b times theta-dot; b is not calibrated to a physical pendulum.
The displayed T0 and omega0 are explicitly undamped small-angle reference quantities; they are not the damped nonlinear animation period.
The integrator is a numerical fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme with bounded internal time steps.
scientificEvidence.benchmarkScope: Analytical closed-form reference vectors only. These confirm code-to-equation consistency for the declared input case; they are not measured data, calibration, uncertainty quantification or validation of real-world predictive accuracy.

itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: F=−kx; omega=sqrt(k/m); T=2pi sqrt(m/k)
itemLevelCitations.limitations: Applies to an ideal linear spring and small enough deformation for Hooke's law.

declaredAssumptions: The spring obeys a linear Hooke's-law force over the full declared displacement range.
The oscillator is one-dimensional with fixed mass and spring constant.
Damping, friction, air resistance and spring mass are neglected.
Total mechanical energy remains constant only under the conservative idealization.

itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: I=U/R for a resistor with a linear current-voltage relation

declaredAssumptions: The circuit is a DC ideal voltage source in series with a fixed ohmic resistor.
Resistance remains constant over the modeled operating range; self-heating does not feed back into resistance.
The readout's one-minute heat is P multiplied by 60 seconds at constant power.
The particle-flow animation is illustrative and is not a microscopic charge-transport simulation.

itemLevelCitations.locator: Section 6.2, static/kinetic friction on an inclined plane and Example 6.11
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: Normal force mg cos(theta), downslope gravity mg sin(theta), and kinetic-friction magnitude fk=mu_k N
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The reference treats static and kinetic coefficients as distinct; the prototype uses one shared mu for both the slip threshold and sliding friction, which is a deliberate simplifying assumption rather than a fully validated friction law.

declaredAssumptions: The incline is rigid and planar, with constant gravitational acceleration.
The object is treated as a rigid body with no rotation or rolling.
Air resistance, vibration and contact compliance are neglected.
A single coefficient mu is used for both the static slip threshold and kinetic friction; real contacts generally require distinct mu_s and mu_k values.
The kinetic-friction law is an empirical approximation, not a universal material law.

declaredAssumptions: The thermodynamic calculations use the ideal-gas approximation.
The average kinetic energy is translational kinetic energy per molecule, not total molecular internal energy including rotations or vibrations.

The rendered particles are visual markers whose speed is scaled for animation; they do not represent measured molecular trajectories or solve molecular collisions.
Pressure is calculated using pV=nRT; it is not inferred from counting simulated particle-wall impacts.

declaredAssumptions: Both acid and base are treated as strong electrolytes with complete dissociation.
Neutralization stoichiometry is one mole H+ per mole OH− for the represented monoprotic pair.
Solution volumes are assumed additive.

Activities are approximated by concentrations; non-ideal activity coefficients and ionic-strength effects are neglected.

itemLevelCitations.locator: Section 12.5, Arrhenius equation and two-temperature form
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: k=A exp(−Ea/RT), with activation energy in J/mol, gas constant in J/(mol·K) and absolute temperature in kelvin
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The prototype's A=1 s^-1 and Ea values of 70/40 kJ mol^-1 are illustrative model settings, not experimentally fitted parameters; reaction-specific mechanism and rate law are not established.

declaredAssumptions: The rate constant follows a single Arrhenius expression over the represented temperature interval.
The pre-exponential factor is fixed at A=1 s^-1 for an illustrative first-order model, not fitted from experimental data.
Activation energies 70 kJ/mol without catalyst and 40 kJ/mol with catalyst are illustrative chosen values, not measured or literature-derived for a named reaction.
The rate law v=kc is first-order in the represented concentration; no reaction mechanism or concentration-dependent activity coefficient is modeled.
The animation's collision flashes are visual heuristics, not stochastic collision kinetics or measured reaction events.

scientificEvidence.benchmarkScope: Analytical closed-form reference vectors only. These confirm code-to-equation consistency for the declared input case; they are not measured data, calibration, uncertainty quantification or validation of real-world predictive accuracy.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §3.5, equations 3.15–3.17; set initial vertical velocity to zero and solve the constant-g equations for the ground-impact time and speed
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: v=gt; h=(1/2)gt²; t=sqrt(2h/g); impact speed=sqrt(2gh)
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The equations assume negligible air resistance and approximately constant g. Contact with the ground ends free fall.

declaredAssumptions: The body is released from rest with zero initial vertical velocity.
Motion is one-dimensional and vertical.
Gravity is constant over the fall and air resistance, wind and buoyancy are neglected.
The object stops being in free fall at ground contact; the model does not simulate impact or rebound.
The displayed kinetic-energy readout assumes a reference mass of 1 kg rather than a user-supplied physical object mass.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §3.5, equations 3.15–3.17; upward-positive sign convention with constant acceleration −g
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: v(t)=v0−gt; y(t)=v0t−(1/2)gt²; t_up=v0/g; Hmax=v0²/(2g); same-elevation flight time=2v0/g
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The total flight-time formula assumes return to the launch elevation. Air resistance is neglected.

declaredAssumptions: The object is launched vertically upward and returns to the same elevation from which it was launched.
The only acceleration during flight is a constant downward gravitational acceleration g.
Air resistance, wind, buoyancy and lift are neglected.
The highest point is an instantaneous zero-vertical-velocity state, not a period of hovering.
The animation is one-dimensional and does not model launch mechanics or impact.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §4.4, equations 4.27–4.30; centripetal acceleration ac=v²/r and angular-frequency parameterization
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: ac=v²/r; Fc=mac; period T=2πr/v; angular speed omega=v/r
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The equations describe ideal circular motion. The displayed Fc value uses a fixed illustrative mass of 1 kg; actual inward force depends on the real system and may be supplied by tension, gravity, friction, contact force, or their resultant.

declaredAssumptions: The object follows a circle with fixed radius and constant tangential speed.
The path is planar and no radial displacement or change in radius is modeled.
The force readout uses a fixed illustrative mass of 1 kg because mass is not an input parameter.
Centripetal force denotes the net inward force component; it is not an extra force to be added to real force diagrams.
Tangential acceleration is zero in the uniform-speed mode.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §4.3, horizontal launch from a nonzero height; combine constant horizontal velocity with vertical free fall and solve for impact time
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: x=v0t; h=(1/2)gt²; t=sqrt(2h/g); R=v0 sqrt(2h/g); impact speed=sqrt(vx²+vy²)
itemLevelCitations.limitations: Assumes negligible air resistance and constant g. Unlike the standard same-level range formula, this case lands below the launch elevation.

declaredAssumptions: The launch is horizontal, so the initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is constant downward at g.
The projectile lands on a flat horizontal surface at a vertical drop equal to h.
Air resistance, wind, spin, lift and obstacles are neglected.
The animation does not model the launch device or impact dynamics.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §4.3, equations 4.24–4.26; time of flight, parabolic trajectory and range for launch and impact at the same elevation
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: x=v0 cos(theta)t; y=v0 sin(theta)t−(1/2)gt²; T=2v0 sin(theta)/g; R=v0² sin(2theta)/g; Hmax=v0² sin²(theta)/(2g)
itemLevelCitations.limitations: Same-elevation range and 45° maximum apply only when launch and impact heights are equal and air resistance is neglected.

declaredAssumptions: The projectile is launched and lands at the same vertical elevation.
Gravity is uniform and constant during the trajectory.
Air resistance, wind, spin, lift and buoyancy are neglected.
Horizontal and vertical components are independent; horizontal velocity remains constant.
The 45° maximum-range statement is conditional on same-level landing and the no-drag idealization.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §3.4, constant-acceleration kinematics with a=0; average velocity equals constant velocity
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: x=vt; t=L/v for a one-dimensional constant-speed trajectory of length L
itemLevelCitations.limitations: This is the zero-acceleration limiting case of the kinematic equations; the model assumes the direction remains fixed and does not describe acceleration phases.

declaredAssumptions: Velocity is constant in both magnitude and direction throughout the represented path.
Acceleration is zero; start-up, braking and turning transients are not modeled.
The route is one-dimensional and its length L is measured along the path.
The displayed average velocity equals the constant signed velocity only because direction does not change.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §3.4, equations 3.12–3.14; velocity-time relation and displacement for constant acceleration
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: v=v0+at; x=v0t+(1/2)at²; v²=v0²+2ax
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The equations require constant acceleration over the modeled time interval and a consistent one-dimensional sign convention.

declaredAssumptions: Motion is one-dimensional with constant acceleration a over the entire interval.
The acceleration sign follows the chosen positive coordinate direction; the current default is positive.
The model does not include velocity-dependent drag, changing net force, mass variation or staged acceleration.
The displacement formula assumes the initial position is the zero reference for the displayed distance.

itemLevelCitations.locator: §3.5, equations 3.15–3.17; apply constant-g vertical kinematics with the positive coordinate chosen downward
itemLevelCitations.formulaCoverage: v=v0+gt; h=v0t+(1/2)gt²; positive impact time t=(sqrt(v0²+2gh)−v0)/g
itemLevelCitations.limitations: The equations assume negligible air resistance, constant g and motion only until the object reaches the lower reference surface.

declaredAssumptions: The object is launched vertically downward with initial speed v0.
The positive coordinate is selected downward, so gravity contributes +g.
Gravity is constant and air resistance, wind, buoyancy and lift are neglected.
The object is evaluated only until it has fallen through the specified vertical distance h.
Impact, deformation, rebound and energy dissipation on contact are not modeled.
